questions.learningObjective: Explain why an idea's origin does not settle its truth
questions.stem: Stage 1: Ticket ENG-253 dismisses the retry jitter because it came from a game engine.

options.text: Game engines are always wrong for services.
Game-engine origin does not show jitter is wrong.

questions.explanation: Where jitter came from does not decide whether it helps. It should be tested against this system's retry behavior.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Spot pity used to bypass evidence in a ticket
questions.stem: Ticket ENG-254 urges keeping a broken build because fixing it would upset the release manager.

options.text: Feelings prove the build is fine.
Upsetting someone does not justify keeping a broken build.

questions.explanation: A release manager's feelings do not make a broken build acceptable. The build needs fixing based on failure evidence.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Recognize popularity mistaken for correctness
questions.stem: Ticket ENG-255 says the new layout must ship because most internal staff like it.

answer.exemplar: Internal staff liking the layout does not show it works for customers; the team should test with target users and accessibility checks before shipping.

questions.explanation: Internal popularity is not proof of customer fit. External usability evidence is needed.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Identify fear used to force a change

stimulus.body: Ticket ENG-256 demands removing the feedback widget, warning that any delay will cause a PR disaster. No sentiment or usage data is attached.

questions.stem: In ticket ENG-256, what is the logical weakness?

options.text: It shows the widget is unused.
It proves the widget harms PR.
It uses PR fear to force removal without data.

questions.explanation: A feared PR disaster is asserted without sentiment or usage data. Fear cannot replace evidence about the widget's effect.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish coincidence from causation in a ticket

stimulus.body: Ticket ENG-257 blames the new tooltip for a drop in clicks because clicks fell after tooltips shipped. No experiment isolated tooltips.

questions.stem: Stage 1: What is the core flaw in ticket ENG-257?

options.text: It blames tooltips from timing without an experiment.

questions.explanation: Clicks falling after tooltips shipped does not prove tooltips caused it. An experiment is needed to isolate the effect.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Recognize after-this-therefore-because-of-this
questions.stem: Stage 1: Ticket ENG-258 says latency improved after the team added caching, so caching fixed latency.

options.text: Sequence alone does not prove caching caused the improvement.

questions.explanation: Latency improving after caching was added does not show causation. Other changes in the same window could explain it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Spot an unchecked chain of consequences
questions.stem: Ticket ENG-259 opposes a single A/B test, claiming it will lead to endless experiments and chaos.

options.text: It predicts chaos from one test without evidence.

questions.explanation: A slide from one A/B test to chaos is asserted without showing governance cannot prevent it. Each step needs evidence.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Identify an attack on the speaker instead of the claim
questions.stem: Ticket ENG-260 rejects the rollback plan because its author, Priya, once argued against rollbacks.

answer.exemplar: Priya's past opposition to rollbacks does not refute this rollback plan; it should be evaluated on its triggers, steps, and recovery criteria.

questions.explanation: A past stance by Priya does not make the plan wrong. The plan's content is the proper review target.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an idea's origin does not settle its truth

stimulus.body: Ticket ENG-261 dismisses the new retry cap because it was borrowed from a mobile app. No load test is cited.

questions.stem: In ticket ENG-261, what fallacy is committed?

options.text: It proves mobile apps fail on servers.
It shows the cap is too low.
It rejects the cap based on origin, not load data.

questions.explanation: Where the cap came from does not decide whether it works. Load testing against this system's traffic is needed.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Spot pity used to bypass evidence in a ticket

stimulus.body: Ticket ENG-262 urges keeping a redundant service because removing it would make an on-call engineer sad. No usage or cost data is attached.

questions.stem: Stage 1: What fallacy drives ticket ENG-262?

options.text: It proves the service is needed.
It uses pity to keep a redundant service.
It shows the engineer is wrong.

questions.explanation: An engineer's sadness does not make a redundant service worth keeping. Usage and cost evidence should decide.
